This is Abū Jaʿfar Muḥammad ibn Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥasan, known by the title Khwāja Naṣīr al-Dīn al-Ṭūsī, after the city of Ṭūs in Khurasan (597–673 AH/1200–1274 CE). He was one of the leading Islamic philosophers of the seventh century AH/thirteenth century CE and one of the outstanding scholars of natural science, astronomy, and mathematics in his age. His works include a commentary on Ibn Sīnā’s Pointers and Reminders. See Shaykh ʿAbd Allāh Niʿma, The Shiʿi Philosophers, Beirut, no date, p. 472 ff.↩︎

After Ibn Sīnā’s explicit statements that what is brought into existence “is not preceded by non-existence,” it is surprising to find a major scholar of philosophy such as Dr. Ibrāhīm Madkūr commenting on Ibn Sīnā’s view that the heavenly world is “brought into existence” by saying that “bringing into existence means creation from nothing.” The idea of creation from nothing is fundamentally foreign to Ibn Sīnā’s philosophy. Another piece of evidence for the eternity of time in Ibn Sīnā is his statement: “Time is not brought into existence through a temporal coming-to-be. Rather, it comes into existence through origination, in which its originator does not precede it in time or duration, but only in essence (...). Time is therefore originated—that is, its Creator [originator] precedes it only....” The passage goes on to say that motion, like time, also does not come into being through a temporal beginning. It too is originated in this special sense, or comes into being through essential rather than temporal origination. This is another way of expressing the eternity of time and motion. See The Salvation, pp. 117, 301. Carra de Vaux misunderstood this point in Ibn Sīnā when he judged it “naive from the intellectual point of view” (Carra de Vaux, Avicenna, trans. ʿĀdil Zuʿaytir, p. 185). He may not have taken account of Ibn Sīnā’s doctrine of “origination,” on which the idea of “originated” time rests. Ibn Sīnā’s purpose in this doctrine is precisely to affirm the eternity of what is originated in this sense, whether matter, motion, or time.↩︎

The Salvation, p. 253. Notice Ibn Sīnā’s phrase, “it has become clear to us in natural science....” This is further evidence for our claim that his philosophical structure rests on what he had learned about the laws of nature.↩︎

Ibn Sīnā states this proposition in another form that may be clearer and more direct, though the meaning is the same. He says: “Renewal is possible only with a change of state. A change of state is possible only where there is a capacity for change—that is, a subject. This continuity therefore belongs to motion and to something moving—that is, to change and something changing....” Pointers and Reminders, vol. 3, p. 100. This statement also shows that change is motion, and that the changing thing is the subject of motion—the thing that moves, namely matter. Ibn Sīnā then explains the unity of motion and time within the subject, matter. He says that this continuity connected with motion and the moving thing can be measured, meaning that the quantity of change can be known. This is time: the measure of motion not in terms of distance, but in terms of before and after. Same source.↩︎

Engels says in this connection that theoretical thought in every age—including our own—is a historical product and takes on very different forms and contents. It was on this basis that he valued so highly the view of nature as a whole found among the great founders of Greek philosophy. On the same basis, he made his well-known statement about the historical character of modern ideas, in a sense very different from what is meant by those who try to “modernize” the heritage: the various forms of Greek philosophy already contain, in embryonic and developing form, most of the later kinds of worldview. See Dialectics of Nature, Arabic ed., pp. 45, 61, 66.↩︎

Ibn Sīnā explains the difference between first and second perfections as follows: “The perfections of natural bodies are either first perfections, whose disappearance causes the thing they perfect to cease to be what it is, or second perfections, whose disappearance does not destroy the thing itself but only makes its condition less complete” (same source).↩︎

Ibn Sīnā regards matter as a substance. Among his statements to this effect is: “Accidents come after matter by nature (...), while matter and form come before accidents by nature and causally” (The Salvation, p. 99). By contrast, he denies that motion is a substance. For example, he says: “Every motion is something that can increase and decrease, while no substance is like that. Therefore no motion is a substance” (The Salvation, p. 105). The basis of this denial is clear: substance is treated as static, while motion consists precisely in change and instability, since it can increase and decrease. Substance, on this view, is fixed and does not admit increase, decrease, transformation, or opposites in itself.↩︎
By “metaphysical” here we mean the opposite of “dialectical,” not the opposite of “physical” or natural.↩︎

Ibn Sīnā says in Pointers and Reminders (vol. 2, pp. 65–66): “As for forms that leave matter and are replaced by others, they cannot be called absolute causes of the one continuous existence that preserves its identity.” This indicates that succession through replacement—that is, change and transformation—takes place within one continuing subject. The subject of changing motion here is therefore substance, or matter.↩︎

In this connection Ibn Sīnā says that “the coming-to-be and passing-away of substances are not motion; they occur all at once (...). Motion exists in time between pure potentiality and pure actuality, and is not one of those things that reaches a stable and complete state of actuality” (The Salvation, p. 105). On this basis he distinguishes generation from alteration in The Healing, natural philosophy section, Generation and Corruption, Cairo ed., 1969, p. 224.↩︎

Although Ibn Sīnā is generally known to question whether motion occurs in the categories of quality and quantity, here he says that it does occur in both, just as it occurs in the categories of place and position. He limits motion in quality to qualities that can become weaker or more intense, such as whiteness and blackness. As for position, he says that in his own view it does admit motion: the rotation of a round body around itself. We find no motion in the category of time, because matter has time only through motion itself. See The Salvation, pp. 101–107.↩︎

See same source, p. 209. This statement by Ibn Sīnā supports Hādī al-ʿAlawī’s conclusion in The Theory of Substantial Motion in al-Shīrāzī, Baghdad, 1971, p. 18: some of what ancient philosophers, including the Arabs, placed under the category of substance reflects their awareness of the objective relation between different aspects of phenomena. Dividing existence into substances and accidents points to an attempt to distinguish what is basic and stable from what is accidental, or to distinguish the content that gives a phenomenon its particular nature from what is external or merely formal, however necessary it may be.↩︎

In ancient terminology, the difference between ṭabʿ and ṭabīʿa is this: ṭabīʿa, “nature,” is a principle of motion in the thing itself without awareness, while ṭabʿ is a principle in the more general sense, whether or not awareness is involved. See Sulaymān Dunyā’s notes on Pointers and Reminders, vol. 2, p. 161.↩︎

According to the Neoplatonic theory of emanation, the “separate intellects” are the first intellects that emanate in sequence from the First Being, God, from the first intellect through the tenth, the active intellect. They are simple substances. In the original Neoplatonic theory, they are called “separate” because “simple” here means not joined to matter—in other words, separate from it. With Ibn Sīnā, however, this “separation” takes on a new meaning. We will return to this point.↩︎

Al-Fārābī, The Opinions of the People of the Virtuous City, ed. Nādir, Beirut, 1959, p. 44. Al-Fārābī makes the multiplicity within the separate intellect twofold, while Ibn Sīnā makes it threefold. Al-Fārābī’s twofold scheme works as follows: from the First, God, there proceeds a first intellect. Insofar as this intellect thinks its principle, God, a second intellect proceeds from it; insofar as it thinks itself, the “first heaven” proceeds from it. The same pattern continues through the remaining intellects. From each intellect in sequence, in addition to the next intellect, there also proceeds a star or a celestial sphere. These spheres arise in the following order: the sphere of the fixed stars, Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, the Sun, Venus, Mercury, and the Moon.↩︎
